Chapter 1: Ordinary Lives Before the Disaster
Before everything changed, life in the towns and villages around Chernobyl moved at its own gentle pace. You’d hear roosters crowing before sunrise, kids rushing off to school, and workers heading out—to the fields or, for many, to the power plant itself. That nuclear station was more than just a workplace. It was a beacon of progress and hope, with its cooling towers standing tall at the edge of Pripyat, promising a brighter tomorrow.
Back then, the plant felt like just another part of the landscape. Families built their routines around it—celebrating birthdays, planning weddings, even daydreaming about vacations. Pripyat, the city created for the plant’s workers, was alive and buzzing. Picture parks filled with laughter, cinemas showing the latest films, playgrounds echoing with children’s shouts. Living there felt like a stroke of luck, surrounded by all the comforts Soviet life could offer.
One mother, for example, cherished the everyday joys: her child’s laughter bouncing off the apartment walls, the smell of fresh bread wafting from the bakery downstairs, the excitement of waiting for a brand-new television set. A young technician, proud to wear his uniform, felt a rush of satisfaction at the respect it brought. And for the older folks, the plant was a symbol—proof that their sacrifices during the war and those tough years after had built something truly remarkable.
But if you listened closely, there was a hint of unease under the surface. Some workers noticed strange things—alarms that rang for no reason, instructions that didn’t always add up, and a workplace culture where asking questions wasn’t exactly encouraged. Still, most people brushed those worries aside. They’d been told the plant was safe. The experts had it all under control. Life simply carried on.
The daily routines—shopping, tending gardens, chatting with neighbors—helped everyone feel secure. People made plans for the future, never guessing how quickly everything could change. When disaster finally arrived, it didn’t just tear down buildings or poison the land. It shattered the very idea of what was normal, leaving behind a world where even the air felt dangerous to breathe.
That’s what makes these early memories so striking. The simple, ordinary days before the explosion make the disaster that followed seem almost unreal. It’s easy to forget—disasters rarely give warning. They hit right in the middle of everyday life, turning what’s familiar into something you barely recognize.
